parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Start by looking at where the two op-amp inputs are connected in Fig. 7.1. What is the potential of the + input, and what is point P connected to?
Hint 2: Recall the size of the open-loop gain of an ideal op-amp and how output voltage is related to the difference between the two inputs.
Hint 3: Think about what would happen if there was even a tiny voltage difference between P and earth. Would the output stay within the +9.0 V to -9.0 V supply limits?
Hint 4: Link negative feedback through R2 to how any difference is automatically corrected, leaving P at almost 0 V without being directly wired to earth.
parts.proper_answer: Ideal op-amp has very large open-loop gain. V+ is connected to earth so V+ = 0 V. Since $V_{OUT} = A(V+ - V-)$, for $V_{OUT}$ not to saturate, $(V+ - V-)$ must be essentially zero. Hence $V- \approx V+ = 0$ V, so point P is at earth potential but not directly earthed, a virtual earth maintained by negative feedback.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the earthed input**
You can see in Fig. 7.1 that the non-inverting input marked + is wired straight to the earth line. That means $V+ = 0\text{ V}$ all the time. Point P is wired to the inverting input marked -, so the voltage at P is $V-$.

Step 2: **Remember how huge the gain is**
For any op-amp, $$V_{OUT} = A_0 \times (V+ - V-)$$ where $A_0$ is the open-loop gain. For an ideal op-amp $A_0$ is taken as infinite, in practice very large, e.g. $10^5$.

Step 3: **See why the inputs must be almost equal**
The output cannot exceed the supply rails of $+9.0\text{ V}$ to $-9.0\text{ V}$. If $(V+ - V-)$ was even a millivolt, $A_0$ times that would try to drive the output to thousands of volts and it would saturate. So in normal linear operation with negative feedback, $$(V+ - V-) \approx 0$$

Step 4: **Explain virtual earth**
Since $V+ = 0\text{ V}$, then $V- \approx 0\text{ V}$ too. Point P therefore sits at about earth potential. It is called virtual because it is not directly connected to earth, it is held there by the action of the feedback through $R_2$. If $V-$ tries to rise, the output goes negative and pulls it back down until $V- = V+$ when stable.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Use the virtual earth result from (i) to write down the potential at P, then think about the p.d. across R1 between VIN and P.
Hint 2: Recall the ideal op-amp property for current entering the inputs, and decide what this means for the current through R1 compared to the current through R2.
Hint 3: Write Ohm's law $I = V/R$ separately for the current in R1 and the current in R2, taking care with signs for VOUT.
Hint 4: Equate the two currents and rearrange to get $V_{OUT}/V_{IN}$ in terms of R1 and R2 only.
parts.proper_answer: Ideal op-amp has infinite input impedance so no current enters P. Current in $R_1$ = current in $R_2$. With $V_P = 0$, $I = (V_{IN}-0)/R_1 = (0-V_{OUT})/R_2$. Hence gain $G = V_{OUT}/V_{IN} = -R_2/R_1$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use no current into the op-amp**
An ideal op-amp has infinite input impedance, so essentially zero current flows into the - input at P. That is really helpful because the current arriving through $R_1$ has nowhere else to go except through $R_2$. So $$I_{R1} = I_{R2} = I$$

Step 2: **Write the current in R1**
Left end of $R_1$ is at $V_{IN}$, right end at P which is at $0\text{ V}$ from the virtual earth idea. The p.d. across $R_1$ is $V_{IN} - 0$. By Ohm's law: $$I = \frac{V_{IN} - 0}{R_1}$$

Step 3: **Write the current in R2**
Left end of $R_2$ is at P ($0\text{ V}$), right end is at $V_{OUT}$. The p.d. from P to output is $0 - V_{OUT}$, driving the same current $I$ through $R_2$: $$I = \frac{0 - V_{OUT}}{R_2}$$

Step 4: **Equate and find gain**
Equating the two expressions for $I$: $$\frac{V_{IN}}{R_1} = \frac{-V_{OUT}}{R_2}$$ Rearranging for the closed-loop voltage gain: $$\frac{V_{OUT}}{V_{IN}} = -\frac{R_2}{R_1}$$ The minus sign shows inversion: a positive input gives a negative output.

parts.label: (b)
key_concepts: transfer of input waveform to output
hints: Hint 1: First find the numerical voltage gain from your expression in (a)(ii) using $R_2/R_1 = 4.5$, and note its sign.
Hint 2: Calculate what $V_{OUT}$ would be without limits when $V_{IN} = 3.0\text{ V}$, and compare with the -9.0 V supply to see that saturation must occur.
Hint 3: Work out the input voltage at which saturation just starts, then sketch how $V_{OUT}$ falls from zero, clips flat, then rises back as $V_{IN}$ falls.
parts.proper_answer: Gain $= -4.5$. Unsaturated $V_{OUT} = -4.5 V_{IN}$. Saturation at $-9.0\text{ V}$ occurs when $V_{IN} = 2.0\text{ V}$. $V_{OUT}$ is an inverted ramp from 0 to $-9.0\text{ V}$, then flat at $-9.0\text{ V}$ while $V_{IN} > 2.0\text{ V}$, then ramp back to 0 in step with $V_{IN}$ falling to 0.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the gain and ideal output**
From (a)(ii): $$G = -\frac{R_2}{R_1} = -4.5$$ So ideally $$V_{OUT} = -4.5 \times V_{IN}$$ A positive-going $V_{IN}$ gives a negative-going $V_{OUT}$ with 4.5 times the size.

Step 2: **Find where clipping starts**
The output cannot go more negative than the $-9.0\text{ V}$ rail. Set the ideal value equal to the rail: $$-4.5 \times V_{IN} = -9.0$$ $$V_{IN} = 2.0\text{ V}$$ From Fig. 7.2, $V_{IN}$ rises from 0 to $3.0\text{ V}$, so for all $V_{IN}$ above $2.0\text{ V}$ the output is stuck at $-9.0\text{ V}$.

Step 3: **Describe the waveform to draw**
Starting at $t=0$, $V_{OUT}=0$. As $V_{IN}$ ramps up, $V_{OUT}$ ramps down linearly with 4.5 times steeper slope until it hits $-9.0\text{ V}$ at the time $V_{IN}$ reaches $2.0\text{ V}$. It then stays horizontal at $-9.0\text{ V}$ while $V_{IN}$ goes up to $3.0\text{ V}$, stays at $3.0\text{ V}$, and starts to fall. When $V_{IN}$ falls back below $2.0\text{ V}$, $V_{OUT}$ leaves saturation and ramps linearly back up to 0 at the same time $V_{IN}$ reaches 0.
